body:
You are drafting DIALOGUE LINES for a video game. Reply in plain text only, in the exact format asked. No commentary.

## The game
"The Crooked Moon" is a single-player turn-based tactical party RPG (fully voiced, branching dialogue, skill checks, a storyteller Narrator). Folk-horror campaign set in Druskenvald, an afterlife realm of endless night under a gargantuan crescent moon with a leering crone's face. Drawn like a 1960s monster cartoon stuck in Halloween, but the story is real folk horror: stakes, doomed innocents, sacrifice. Humour is deadpan and sits inside the dread. Everything is our own invention in our own words.

## This chapter: Maidenmist Cemetery
South-east of the village of Wickermoor, an endless fogbound cemetery fenced with cold iron is really a prison built over a tear into the Shroud, the mist of death that rings the realm. Wrathful soul-stripped spirits called the shrouded would pour out of it. Its sexton is YORGRIM, the ghost of an orc seer of the Shadestone Clan, who was tricked by his chieftain into a ritual that annihilated his whole clan's souls; he drags a gravestone carved with their names chained to his back as penance. He is dour, stoic, few words, never cruel, tells what matters, and grows vaguer and more distracted as the chapter goes; deep slow orc bass, short flat sentences, long pauses. His spectral black hound ISOLDE (white eyes, a hooded lantern in her mouth) does not speak: only the Narrator describes her. He asked five friends to kindle balefire beacons from fragments of their souls: Sir Marius Renathyr (knight of a morning god, horse Dawn, King Viktor Denathria), Lethica Nightborne (priestess of the Nightmother, barn owl, loved Marius), Ol' Jericho Sticks (kindly scarecrow banjo man), Captain Briggsy Kratch (pirate with a heart of gold, lucky, a swordsman and schemer), Farryn of the Greenwood (satyr druid of the Green Queen, loved Gwenna). They fell to the Horned King's sin and the heroes (the player's party of four, level nine) killed them. The beacons went dark, the tear grew, the dead walked into Wickermoor. The heroes relight the beacons with Final Rites that honour who the Fallen were before they fell, then go below, where Yorgrim breaks and becomes the Chained Reaper; they destroy him and perform his own rites to seal the tear.
Wickermoor people: MORI SHADE, undertaker, grave, stately, white hair, all black, a fount of folklore, follows the Strangers' ways learned from Yorgrim; DORIS SQUIRE, constable, tall, stocky, says the fewest words possible, flat northern burr; TOBIAS DIBBS, Mori's apprentice, relentlessly cheerful and practical; HESTER BOLTON, annoyed her husband Gregor is now a ghast and still owes rent; ADELA DRUSKENVALD (transatlantic 1920s patter); WESTON MURDOCH (warm revival preacher); Theodora Mayville the postmaster is secretly a pigeon hag.

## The Narrator
The Narrator is the Vagrant, a frog-faced ferryman telling the tale afterwards: warm, folksy, wry, fond of the party; never gloats. Second person, present tense, only what a hero could perceive, concrete senses (smell, sound, texture), no game words (HP, roll, level, check, DC, save), no modern slang, never "suddenly". Never name a specific hero (the party is addressed as "you" or "the party").

## Format rules
- One line of plain text per key, written as `key: text`. No quotes around the text, no stage directions, no asterisks, no emoji, no em dashes (use commas, periods, colons), straight quotes only, no brackets.
- A spoken line is one to three short sentences, 12 to 38 words, never over 45. Narrator lines are one or two sentences, never over 45 words. People speak plainly in their own voice; they do not explain the plot to the audience.
- Obey each brief's sentence count and content. Every line must carry a concrete detail.
- Do not put speaker names at the start of the text. Do not repeat the brief.


## Lines to draft (key | speaker | mood | brief). Reply with one `key: text` line for each key and nothing else.

grammar_correct | Narrator | - | The headstone sighs through its entire carved face and fixes the spelling in the air. One sentence.
names_start | mori_shade | neutral | Mori has three unmarked graves in the Potter's Field and a ledger of villagers who lost someone; match the names, give each grave its stone. Three short sentences.
names_graves | Narrator | - | Three plain posts stand in a row, each with a small token left at its foot. One sentence.
names_a | Narrator | - | The first token is a corner of a baker's apron; a grave of Holly Aster's mother. One sentence.
names_a_plain | Narrator | - | The first token is a scrap of cloth and could be anyone's. One sentence.
names_b | Narrator | - | The second token is a child's wooden toy; a grave of a Lockwood child Old Rusty remembers. One sentence.
names_b_plain | Narrator | - | The second token is a toy, worn smooth; it says nothing of whose. One sentence.
names_c | Narrator | - | The third token is a thimble stamped with a tailor's mark; a grave of someone Thomasin Ardor lost. One sentence.
names_c_plain | Narrator | - | The third token is a thimble with no mark you can read. One sentence.
names_mori | mori_shade | neutral | Mori reads the ledger and matches all three tokens to names, and says each should hear of it in person. Two short sentences.
names_holly | Narrator | - | Holly Aster sets down her tray and says her mother's name aloud for the first time in years. One sentence.
names_rusty | Narrator | - | Old Rusty stops sweeping and says a child's name that nobody has said on the hill since. One sentence.
names_thomasin | Narrator | - | Thomasin Ardor holds the thimble in both hands and does not say anything for a long time. One sentence.
names_done | mori_shade | smile | Mori says the three graves have names and the field will remember. Two short sentences.
names_wait | mori_shade | neutral | Mori says some of the three still wait to be told. One short sentence.
names_drop | mori_shade | sad | Mori says the posts will stay blank, and the field will keep forgetting. Two short sentences.
walk_ask | Narrator | - | Isolde stands in the doorway of the sepulcher and tugs the hem of a coat, turning to look at the sites and back. One or two sentences.
walk_yes | Narrator | - | Isolde sets off down the nearest path, looking back every few steps to see the party follows. One sentence.
walk_no | Narrator | - | Isolde lowers herself to the step and watches the path with her ears flat. One sentence.
walk_leave | Narrator | - | Isolde does not follow. By morning her lantern has gone dark by the door. One sentence.
walk_site | Narrator | - | Isolde stops at the old brazier, noses at something hidden in the ash, and waits. One sentence.
walk_end | Narrator | - | At the Shadestone stones Isolde noses up a packet wrapped in oilcloth: Yorgrim's letter to Mori. One sentence.
adela_1 | adela_druskenvald | smile | Lady Adela Druskenvald, transatlantic, thanks the party for the cemetery and says she thought it had been averted for good. Two sentences.
adela_2 | adela_druskenvald | sly | Adela adds, lightly, that she has seen something in the tower clock; pigeons. One short sentence.
golub_tease | Narrator | - | On the roof of the post office a hundred pigeons shift all together, and Theodora Mayville watches the party pass with violet eyes. One or two sentences.
weston_1 | weston_murdoch | smile | Weston Murdoch, revival-preacher warmth, says the Brightsingers heard the bells and will sing for the dead tonight. Two sentences.
doris_after | doris_squire | neutral | Doris, in as few words as possible, says the village is quiet and she is grateful. Two short sentences.
result:
grammar_correct: The mossy headstone exhales a long sigh through its chiseled letters, and the crooked spelling shifts in the cold air until it reads true.
names_start: Three graves in the Potter's Field still stand with bare cedar posts. My ledger holds the names of everyone our village lost to the mist. Match the tokens left beside them, and we can carve their proper stones.
names_graves: Three unpainted cedar posts stand in a neat row through the wet grass, each with a small keepsake resting in the mud at its foot.
names_a: The first token is a singed corner of a linen baker's apron, still dusted with flour from the hearth of Holly Aster's mother.
names_a_plain: The first token is only a frayed scrap of gray linen, soaked with rain and bearing no mark to show whose hand once held it.
names_b: The second token is a carved wooden horse with one ear chipped away, the sort of pocket toy Old Rusty still remembers a Lockwood child carrying.
names_b_plain: The second token is a small wooden toy worn smooth by rainwater and thumbs, telling you nothing at all of the child who dropped it.
names_c: The third token is a tarnished brass thimble stamped with a tiny shears mark, left in memory of someone dear that Thomasin Ardor lost.
names_c_plain: The third token is a dented brass thimble crusted with dark peat, its rim too worn for your eyes to read any maker's stamp.
names_mori: My ledger matches every one of these small tokens to a name in faded ink. You ought to carry word to their kin in person before I take up the chisel.
names_holly: Holly Aster sets her warm tin tray upon the counter, wipes her floury palms, and speaks her mother's name aloud for the first time in years.
names_rusty: Old Rusty leans on his birch broom in the lane and murmurs a child's name that nobody on the hill has spoken since the fog took them.
names_thomasin: Thomasin Ardor closes both calloused hands around the cold brass thimble and stares at her worktable without speaking a word for a long while.
names_done: Those three graves bear their true names in clean slate at last. Even the damp earth of the Potter's Field will remember who rests under the grass.
names_wait: The names are inked beside my chisel, though some among the bereaved down in Wickermoor still wait to hear the news from your lips.
names_drop: The three cedar posts will stay blank against the rain a while longer. Without a spoken name to anchor it, this field will simply keep forgetting its dead.
walk_ask: Isolde pauses in the stone doorway of the sepulcher and gently tugs the hem of your coat with her teeth. She turns her white eyes toward the dark paths among the graves, then looks back to you.
walk_yes: Isolde trots out along the nearest gravel path with her hooded lantern swinging low, glancing back every few paces to make sure you follow.
walk_no: Isolde lowers her heavy black chest onto the cold stone step and watches the fogbound path with her ears laid flat.
walk_leave: Isolde does not follow you past the iron gate, and by the time morning thins the mist her hooded lantern sits dark beside the sepulcher door.
walk_site: Isolde halts beside the cold iron brazier, noses through the wet gray ash until something glints beneath her snout, and waits for your hand.
walk_end: Beneath the leaning Shadestone markers, Isolde noses a flat packet wrapped in tied oilcloth out of the peat: Yorgrim's final letter to Mori Shade.
adela_1: You have my deepest thanks for settling that dreadful business behind the cemetery iron, darlings. Honestly, I rather thought our little graveyard unpleasantness had been put to bed for good.
adela_2: Though I did spot the queerest flock of gray pigeons roosting inside the tower clockwork this evening.
golub_tease: High on the slate roof of the post office, a hundred gray pigeons shift their feet as one. Below the eaves, Theodora Mayville watches you pass down the lane with gleaming violet eyes.
weston_1: The Brightsingers heard the chapel bells ring clear across the valley mist tonight, my friends. We shall gather every lantern on the steps and sing the weary dead home until dawn.
doris_after: The lane is quiet from the iron gates to the square tonight. You have my thanks for keeping the mist off our cobbles.
